asOf: Close of Friday 2 October 2026 for equities, sectors, bonds, factors and the Treasury curve, with index levels, commodities, currencies and crypto to 05:44 UTC on Monday 5 October

read.headline: 29,000 jobs, a Nasdaq record, and a ten-year that closed higher.
read.standfirst: Friday's September payrolls report gave the market the one thing it had spent a week pricing: 29,000 jobs against about 90,000 expected, a net 60,000 cut to July and August, unemployment up to 4.2% and hourly earnings up only 0.1% on the month. October's hike went to about 22% priced from 64% a week earlier. Stocks rallied: the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.19% to 27,190.86 and the Nasdaq 100 touched a record, the S&P 500 rose 0.73% to 7,722.72 and the Dow 0.49% to 51,176.96, with every sector but health care higher and the Philadelphia semiconductor index up 2.40%. Bonds did not follow: the ten-year closed near 5.27%, about 3bp higher, after Logan said rates need to rise another half point, and the week still ended with the ten-year up about 11bp. Oil eased as the G7 agreed a 100 million barrel stock release and Gulf exports ran above pre-war levels, but Iran says Hormuz stays shut until Washington accepts its plan and a third US carrier group is on its way. Euro-area inflation printed 3.8%, the euro is near its lowest since May 2025, and Tokyo core CPI printed 2.7%. Overnight the Nikkei is up about 2% near 69,700 and Taiwan 2.5%; mainland China and Korea are shut. ISM services at 10:00 ET today.

points.title: Everything in the jobs report pointed at a pause. The curve did not move to meet it.
points.text: The three-month bill is 4.19% and the two-year 4.83%, essentially flat on the week, while the ten-year is 5.28%, up about 11bp, and the thirty-year 5.63%; two-tens is 45bp and bill-to-ten 109bp, the widest of the cycle. October's hike is about 22% priced against 64% a week ago, December is the favoured date and two more moves are priced for the first half of 2027. In the funds the 20-year-plus Treasury fell 0.30% on payrolls day and is 5.75% lower over a month and 10.73% over six; the 7–10 year fund lost 0.28%, municipals 0.37% and mortgage-backed 0.37%, while high yield was flat, senior loans rose 0.10% and convertibles 0.98%. Standard Chartered's Cedric Lam puts the delay in forced selling from hedge funds and property trusts rather than in the Fed. Hammack and Mester say there is time to decide, Goolsbee that every option is open, and Logan that half a point more is needed: the committee has not told the market that September was the last hike.

points.title: Technology led a broad rally: every sector but health care rose, small caps had their best day in nearly a month.
points.text: Consumer discretionary rose 1.13%, technology 1.01%, industrials 0.78%, materials 0.66%, communication services 0.35%, real estate 0.32% and energy 0.19%; health care was flat at −0.01%. Over five sessions technology is +2.07%, energy +2.15% and industrials +1.78% against communication services −0.59% and health care −1.33%, while over a month technology is +6.69% and financials −7.93%, materials −6.83%, utilities −7.54% and real estate −7.10% the weakest. The Philadelphia semiconductor index rose 2.40% and 3.69% on the week, Nvidia touched a record $237.88, and ON Semiconductor jumped about 6.5% on a revised Synaptics deal, while Western Digital and Seagate fell about 10% on a report that Toshiba will double hard-drive capacity. Nike fell about 10% premarket after Thursday's guidance cut and pared much of it. Among the factors the small-cap fund beat the index by 0.39% and the Russell 2000 gained 0.94%, its biggest day in nearly a month; growth beat by 0.33% and is 3.04% ahead over a month while value is 3.13% behind; private equity is 9.90% behind over a month. The VIX closed at 15.31, down 6.59% on the day and 5.37% higher over a month.

points.title: Asia is chasing the Nasdaq record while two of its biggest markets are shut.
points.text: Overnight the Nikkei is up about 2.0% near 69,700 after trading above 70,000 in the morning, Taiwan up about 2.5% near 49,670 and Hong Kong flat after Friday's 2.6% fall, its largest since 23 March, on property and technology; mainland China is shut until 8 October and Korea for a substitute holiday today, so liquidity is thin. In Friday's dollar-denominated country funds Taiwan rose 3.15%, Korea 3.10%, Brazil 2.83%, the Netherlands 1.89%, Mexico 1.88%, Japan 1.58%, France 1.25% and Germany 1.18% while Hong Kong fell 2.66%, China 1.67% and Singapore 0.72%; the emerging-markets fund gained 1.29% and developed ex-US 1.11%. The monthly column is still September's dollar: Turkey −12.62%, Argentina −12.33%, South Africa −11.80%, Indonesia −10.57%, France −7.57%, Mexico −7.23%, Italy −7.21%. Over six months Korea is +56.17% and Taiwan +64.38%, and Korea is +97.37% this year. Europe's Friday bounce — the Stoxx 600 up 0.75% to 631.35 after a four-month low on Thursday — still left it 1.14% lower on the week.

points.title: Brent's columns still straddle the November expiry. The December contract itself is near $102.
points.text: December Brent is $101.73 this morning, down 0.51%, and WTI $90.07, down 1.14%; Friday's settlements were about $91.55 for WTI and about $102.6–102.8 for Brent. The Brent row's five-day +3.77% and one-month +5.66% still start before the November contract's expiry on Wednesday, so they measure the roll as well as the move; since Thursday's Asian open December has risen from about $98 to about $102. What moved it: the G7's agreement on Friday to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from emergency stocks and to avoid export bans, the top OPEC+ producers leaving November quotas unchanged, and Kpler counting Middle East crude exports above their pre-war level of about 18 million barrels a day on several days in late September. Against that, Iran's chief negotiator said Hormuz stays closed until the US accepts Tehran's seven-day plan, shipping agencies report at least one attack a day since Friday, Houthi strikes set an Aramco site near Riyadh ablaze, and a third US carrier group is due by the end of October. Heating oil is $4.54, still up 112.98% this year and 37.77% over three months; gasoline $3.31 is up 92.49%; natural gas $3.02.

points.title: The dollar sits at a 17-month high. The euro is the reason, and France is the reason for the euro.
points.text: The dollar index is about 102, a 17-month high after three straight weekly gains, and EUR/USD is near 1.12, down 0.61% on the day, 1.24% on the week and 3.66% over a month after four consecutive weekly declines and a low since May 2025. French public debt is reported at 119% of output, the 2027 budget with 54 billion euros of savings needs a parliament that does not have a majority for it, ten-year French yields touched their highest since 2002 last week, and Brown Brothers Harriman expects a rollover of this year's budget instead. The euro-area flash inflation print of 3.8% on Friday, a three-year high, made the 29 October ECB meeting harder to call, not easier for the euro. USD/JPY is 158.01, up 0.11%, after a Tokyo core CPI of 2.7% that put an October Bank of Japan move back in the conversation for some economists; the pair is still down 2.51% over three months and the won is 11.87% stronger over three months. The Australian dollar is below 0.69. Bitcoin is $85,750, +2.63% on the week and +7.41% over a month, with Cardano +3.62% on the day and +9.02% on the week.

points.title: Gold is flat at $4,162 after a 7% monthly fall. Sugar and cocoa did the moving.
points.text: Gold is $4,162.00, unchanged on the day, down 0.59% on the week and 7.03% over a month; the Friday settlement on the December future was $4,172.10, down 3.45% on the week. Silver is $61.18, up 1.27%, and platinum $1,725.25, up 1.49%; copper is $6.57, up 0.29%. The agricultural board has its two biggest daily moves of the month: sugar +5.23% to 19.93 and +7.09% on the week, 10.29% over a month and 30.95% over three, and cocoa +5.37% to 5,670, though still 8.37% lower over a month. Lean hogs gained 1.74% and are 28.83% lower over three months; wheat rose 0.65% and is 43.76% higher this year; corn is 7.48% lower over a month; cotton 9.43% lower. The metals have not responded to a weaker payrolls print or a lower hike probability; a dollar at a 17-month high and Treasury yields near multi-decade highs are the reasons usually given.

curve.title: The US Treasury curve
curve.note: Today against a month ago. Friday's payrolls print should have pulled the whole curve down, and for a few minutes it did; the close was higher, because Logan said after the data that rates still need to rise by half a point and the long end was already trading on supply and energy rather than the next Fed decision. Reported closes were about 4.82% on the two-year and 5.27% on the ten, up about 3bp each on the day; the source table prints 4.83%, 5.28% and 5.63%. Over the week the ten-year rose about 11bp and the two-year fell about 3bp, and the ten-year touched 5.344% on Thursday, its highest since 2002. Early Monday the ten-year is near 5.26% and the two-year 4.81%. Coupon supply returns this week: three-year on Tuesday, ten-year on Wednesday, thirty-year on Thursday, with the FOMC minutes on Wednesday afternoon.

spreads.label: 2s10s
spreads.note: 45bp from 46bp on Thursday and 32bp a week ago. The two-year is down about 3bp on the week and the ten-year up about 11bp: the steepening that began when October's hike odds started to fall is now a week old and has not reversed on a payrolls miss.

spreads.label: 3M10Y
spreads.note: 109bp from 107bp on Thursday, the widest stretch of the cycle for a fourth day. The three-month bill is 4.19%, barely changed on the week even as October's hike fell from about 64% to about 22% priced; the ten-year at 5.28% is where the move shows up.

spreads.label: 10s30s
spreads.note: 35bp from 37bp. The twenty-year at 5.67% remains the highest point on the curve, and the thirty-year closed the week at 5.63% after touching 5.642% on Wednesday, its highest since 2002. Mortgage rates are reported near 7.5%.

groups.title: Equities by country
groups.note: Country ETF prices in US dollars at Friday's New York close. Taiwan, Korea and Brazil led the rally; Hong Kong and China fell and Singapore slipped. The five-day column reads +0.92% for the US fund against a weekly index decline of about 0.27%: the source measures it on its own series, so use the index tallies in the text for the week. Monday morning: Nikkei +2.0%, Taiwan +2.5%, Hong Kong flat; Korea and mainland China are shut.

groups.title: US sectors
groups.note: The eleven S&P sector SPDRs at Friday's close. Consumer discretionary +1.13% and technology +1.01% led; every sector but health care (−0.01%) rose. Over a month technology is the only sector in the green, up 6.69%.

groups.title: Bonds and credit
groups.note: Total-return prices, so a falling number means yields rose. Friday's payrolls print did not lift them: the 20-year-plus fund fell 0.30%, the 7–10 year fund 0.28%, municipals and mortgage-backed funds 0.37%. High yield, senior loans and convertibles rose. Every Treasury row is red over a week, a month and three months.

groups.title: Commodities
groups.note: Live to 05:44 UTC on Monday. Brent's row is the December contract; its five-day and one-month columns still start before the November contract expired on Wednesday, so they include the roll. WTI did not roll. Sugar +5.23% and cocoa +5.37% were the day's biggest moves; the G7's 100 million barrel stock release and unchanged OPEC+ quotas leave crude lower on the morning.

groups.title: Currencies
groups.note: Live to Monday morning. The dollar index is at a 17-month high after a third weekly gain; the euro is near its lowest since May 2025 on France's finances and the yen firmed after a hot Tokyo CPI. Read USD/XXX pairs the right way round: a green cell means the dollar gained on that currency, not that the currency did well.

groups.title: Crypto
groups.note: Scaled differently from the rest of the page: a 3% day here is not the event a 3% day in equities is.

groups.title: Factors, against the S&P 500
groups.note: Excess return, not total return. A green cell means the factor beat the index over that window; it does not mean it made money.
